KEY MESSAGE 1...Low-impact weather through Monday night. A few 
thunderstorms are possible Monday afternoon across western portions 
of southern New England.

A weak area of low pressure continues to spin southeast of 
Nantucket, maintaining low clouds and occasional light precipitation 
across the outer Cape and Islands. While not the best beach day 
there, a High Risk for rip currents continues through this evening 
for east-facing beaches of Cape Cod and Nantucket. Elsewhere, most 
of southern New England enjoys sunshine and comfortable conditions. 
The remainder of today through tonight will be relatively quiet. 
Lingering low-level moisture from northeasterly flow combined with 
light winds and mostly clear skies overnight may allow for patchy 
fog to develop in the typical low-lying and river valley locations 
of eastern Massachusetts. Overnight lows fall into the 50s inland 
and the lower 60s along the immediate coast, which is seasonably 
cool for late July.

Monday will feature seasonable temperatures, with highs in the lower 
to middle 80s inland and upper 70s along the coast. A shortwave 
trough dropping into the Northeast, along with an embedded 850-700mb 
disturbance, will provide enough forcing for isolated to scattered 
showers and thunderstorms during the mid to late afternoon, 
primarily west of the Connecticut River Valley. PWATs increase to 
around 1.3 inches, near to slightly above climatological normals but 
not especially anomalous. While a few thunderstorms may produce 
locally heavy downpours, rainfall amounts should generally remain 
modest, with isolated localized totals approaching one-half inch. 
Flash flooding is not anticipated, as 3-hour flash flood guidance 
remains around 2.5 to 3.0 inches. Instability increases to around 
800-1200 J/kg Monday afternoon, but weak deep-layer shear (generally 
less than 30 kt) should limit storm organization. As a result, 
convection is expected to remain isolated and pulse-like, with many 
locations remaining dry. The highest PoPs therefore remain focused 
west of the Connecticut River. CSU machine-learning guidance also 
keeps the better severe-weather signal west of eastern New York. 
While severe weather appears unlikely, the primary hazards with any 
storms will be cloud-to-ground lightning and brief, locally heavy 
rainfall.

Monday night, any lingering convection will diminish during the 
evening. Southwesterly flow aloft then increases moisture, with 
PWATs climbing toward 1.5 inches. Low clouds become more widespread 
overnight, and scattered light showers may begin to develop ahead of 
a more unsettled pattern on Tuesday. Overnight temperatures remain 
mild, holding in the 60s.

KEY MESSAGE 2...Periodic chances of scattered showers and 
thunderstorms early to mid week next week, potentially 
lingering into Thursday. Increasing potential for heavy rain 
late Tuesday through Wednesday with at least localized flash 
flooding possible.

A mid-level trough positions across the region through much of the 
week. A series of shortwaves embedded in the flow are expected to 
progress across the region through the week supporting periodic 
chances for showers and thunderstorms. 

Model guidance has remained generally consistent with a deepening 
trough into Tue/Wed with a strong signal for above normal moisture 
(120-170% of normal) advecting into the region by Tuesday. Most 
deterministic and ensemble solutions have now come on board with the 
development of a low pressure system. In many solutions now, the low 
pressure is quite anomalous in magnitude for late-July. Combined 
with the enhanced forcing from the low, this is a set-up for heavy 
rain potential. However, some model guidance has been more 
aggressive than others. The ECMWF and its ensemble members have 
shown the strongest signal for heavy rain/flash flooding potential 
with a stronger low pressure system tracking in the vicinity of Long 
Island, toward eastern MA/Cape Cod in many of its solutions. It also 
leans on a slower progression of the trough as well. Soundings 
exhibit the textbook environment for efficient rain processes with 
deep warm cloud depths aligned with instability. ECMWF ens probs 
show 40-75% probability for 1+ of rainfall later Tue into Wed and 10-
40% for 2"+ across a good portion of southern New England. The 
deterministic guidance over the last 24 hours of runs has showed a 
large footprint of 2"+ amounts across the region in that same 
timeframe. With weak steering flow this support slow storm motions 
of embedded heavy rain and thunderstorms. This combined with 
potential for training for training will increase the risk for flash 
flooding with more "scattered" occurrences as opposed to an 
isolated case or two. While the recent deterministic runs of the
Canadian and GFS have gone more on board with the heavy rain 
potential, their ensemble guidance still have shown solutions 
leaning toward a weaker low and differing track resulting
